summary: A 1977 revision of the Telnet byte macro option, which lets one side send a short code that stands for a longer string of characters. It replaces RFC 729 and is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The Telnet Byte Macro option lets a sender replace a longer string with one data byte. The receiver first agrees to use the option and accepts each definition, then treats the byte as the full string.

questions: what is the telnet byte macro option
how does telnet bm option work
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets one side use a single byte in place of a longer string.

tldr.problem: Telnet subcommands require at least five characters on the network. For short data blocks, this control information can take up much of the communication.
tldr.mechanism: After negotiating the Byte Macro (BM) option, a sender defines a data byte as shorthand for a replacement string. The receiver expands that byte as if the full string had arrived.
tldr.outcome: The option provides a simple form of data compression and RFC 735 obsoletes RFC 729.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 735 as a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 729. No RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating RFC 735.

sections.title: Why Telnet Uses Byte Macros
sections.content:
A Telnet option subcommand needs at least five characters: IAC SB, the option name, and IAC SE. That overhead may be acceptable for rare commands. It becomes costly when small blocks of data need frequent separators; the control characters can exceed the data itself.

The Byte Macro (BM) option, with command code 19, is intended as a simple way to reduce that overhead. A sender can define a single data character to stand for a longer replacement string.
sections.plainLanguage: When a short block needs a longer control sequence, the control can take more space than the block. A byte macro lets one byte stand for the longer sequence.

sections.title: Agreeing to Use the Option
sections.content:
The option uses Telnet's standard option negotiation. IAC WILL BM says that its sender requests or agrees to send individual data characters that represent replacement strings. IAC DO BM requests or agrees to receive them. WON'T BM and DON'T BM refuse the option and discard existing definitions.

The default is WON'T BM and DON'T BM, so data bytes keep their ordinary meaning until the option is negotiated. The side sending WILL BM controls its definitions, though the other side can refuse a particular one.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must negotiate before a byte can stand for a string. If the option is refused or turned off, each byte keeps its ordinary meaning and the definitions are discarded.

sections.title: Defining and Expanding a Macro
sections.content:
A sender defines a mapping with IAC SB BM DEFINE macro-byte count replacement-string IAC SE. The macro byte can be any 8-bit character except Telnet's IAC character, decimal 255. The count gives the number of replacement characters. The receiver answers with ACCEPT or REFUSE, which may state why it refused. The sender must wait for the answer before using or redefining that macro byte.

After acceptance, the receiver treats the macro byte as the replacement string, except when the byte occurs as part of a Telnet command. Expanded strings are not expanded again, so definitions cannot recursively refer to other macros. LITERAL asks that a macro byte be treated as data; PLEASE CANCEL asks the sender to cancel a definition. The RFC recommends drawing macro bytes from decimal 128 through decimal 254, a range it says is not normally used.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender proposes a byte and the text it represents. After the receiver accepts, that byte means the full text in data, but not inside a Telnet command.
